name: price index
definition: The price level represents the comprehensive average of the prices of various goods and services traded within an economy, weighted according to their relative economic importance. A price index is a normalized macroeconomic metric that captures changes in this price level over time by benchmarking a designated base year's value at 100, serving as a core tool to measure changes in the value of money, convert nominal figures into real values, and observe fluctuations driven by aggregate demand and aggregate supply.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Serves as a vital macroeconomic health indicator alongside economic growth rates and the balance of international payments.  2. Utilized explicitly to measure fluctuations in the cost of living and track broader business cycles.  3. Influenced on the aggregate demand side by variables such as the money supply, household income levels, and expected inflation.  4. Influenced on the aggregate supply side by production factor costs—including wages and international raw material prices—as well as expected inflation.  5. Includes specific localized examples such as South Korea's Consumer Price Index (CPI), Producer Price Index (PPI), Export and Import Price Index, and indices of farm sales and purchase prices.
dict_content: The overall price level, or price, refers to the average of the prices of various goods and services traded in the market, taking into account their importance in economic life. A price index is a measure that represents the change in such prices in the form of an index by setting the price level of a base year as 100 and comparing it with the prices at other points in time. The price index (PI) is an important economic indicator that reflects the macroeconomic movements of a country, along with economic growth and the balance of international payments. Using the price index, one can measure changes in the cost of living or the value of money over a certain period, calculate real amounts from nominal amounts, and gauge economic fluctuations to some extent based on the price level. Prices fluctuate under the influence of aggregate supply and aggregate demand in the economy. Representative factors influencing aggregate demand include the money supply and household income. Prices of production factors, such as wages and international raw material prices, are factors that change aggregate supply, while expected inflation affects both aggregate demand and aggregate supply. Representative price indices in South Korea include the Producer Price Index, Consumer Price Index, Export and Import Price Index, and indices of farm sales and purchase prices.
defense_prompt: 1. The student explains that the price index changes due to market forces but fails to include the structural baseline requirement of a normalized base year. 2. The student attributes a shift in the price level solely to a change in aggregate demand, neglecting how supply-side factor costs or expected inflation shift the equilibrium.

name: inflation
definition: Inflation refers to the macroeconomic phenomenon where the general price level—measured as a collective price index calculated by averaging the prices of individual goods and services—experiences a continuous and sustained increase over time.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Generally recognized as occurring when an annual price increase of around 4-5% is observed. 2. The exact definition can vary depending on different economic perspectives regarding the duration and extent of the price increases. 3. Measurement and definition may consider whether product quality levels have improved over the period. 4. Measurement may account for distortions such as rising prices in black markets caused by government price controls.
dict_content: The phenomenon of the general price level continuously rising is called inflation. Here, the price level refers to the price index calculated by averaging the prices of individual goods. There can be differences of opinion on when to define inflation, considering factors such as the duration and extent of price increases, whether the quality level of products has improved, and whether prices in the black market rise due to government price controls. Generally, when an annual price increase of around 4-5% is observed, it is considered that inflation has occurred.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines inflation merely as a "rise in prices," failing to specify that it must be a continuous and generalized increase rather than a one-time price shock. 2. The student strictly ties the occurrence of inflation to the explicit 4-5% numerical threshold or perfect market conditions, failing to recognize underlying inflationary pressures when prices are artificially suppressed.

name: opportunity cost
definition: Scarcity is the fundamental economic condition where available resources are insufficient to satisfy unlimited human wants, forcing individuals and societies to make choices. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative or benefit that must be foregone when making such a choice. It is an inevitable consequence of scarcity and serves as the core underlying cause of all economic problems.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Benefits considered when calculating opportunity cost can be either tangible or intangible.  2. For a business, an entrepreneur's opportunity cost for an investment includes forgone options such as the bank interest that could have been earned on those investment funds.
dict_content: The phenomenon of resources being insufficient compared to human wants is called scarcity. Since humans cannot satisfy all their desires with scarce resources, everyone must make choices about where to prioritize the use of limited resources. In other words, it means that one has no choice but to select among various desired items. At this time, the best benefit among the expected tangible or intangible benefits from the desires that were given up is called opportunity cost. As long as resource scarcity exists, opportunity cost inevitably occurs, and this becomes the fundamental cause of economic problems. For a business, when an entrepreneur chooses an investment, the value of the other options that were forgone, such as bank interest on the investment funds, becomes the opportunity cost.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines opportunity cost simply as "the cost of choosing an option," omitting the fact that it is specifically the value of the next best rejected alternative. 2. The student overlooks the universal nature of scarcity and assumes opportunity cost only applies to monetary or tangible business decisions.

name: base interest rate
definition: The base rate is the official policy interest rate determined and announced by the central bank (the Bank of Korea). It serves as the fundamental reference rate for all financial transactions between the central bank and commercial financial institutions, directly steering the movement of broader market interest rates—including deposit, loan, and short- to long-term market rates—throughout the economy.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Applies specifically when financial institutions borrow from the Bank of Korea or engage in liquidity-related operations such as fund adjustment loans.  2. Dictates a direct directional relationship where a rise in the base rate causes commercial market rates to rise, and a fall causes them to fall.
dict_content: The base rate is the policy interest rate announced by the Bank of Korea and serves as the reference rate when financial institutions conduct transactions with the Bank of Korea. For example, it applies when financial institutions borrow from the Bank of Korea or engage in transactions such as fund adjustment loans. The base rate affects a variety of interest rates, from ultra-short-term market rates to long- and short-term market rates, as well as deposit and loan rates. When the Bank of Korea announces the base rate, financial institutions, including commercial banks, set their own rates based on it. Therefore, if the base rate rises, market interest rates also rise, and if the base rate falls, market interest rates also fall.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines the base rate merely as the interest rate that commercial banks charge their retail customers for loans and deposits. 2. The student assumes a mechanical, instantaneous transmission where a change in the base rate immediately and perfectly dictates all market rates without commercial bank intervention.

name: compound interest
definition: Compound interest is a method of calculating interest where interest is earned not only on the initial principal but also on the accumulated interest from previous periods. Based on the principle of "interest earning interest," the total value of the principal and interest grows exponentially rather than linearly over time, making the total return significantly higher than that of simple interest as the duration increases.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Utilizes the Rule of 72 to estimate the time or interest rate required to double the investment, where the product of the compounding period and the interest rate equals approximately 72.  2. The compounding frequency can vary, such as semi-annual compounding where interest is added to the principal every 6 months.  3. Incorporates specific numerical examples, such as 100 million won deposited for 2 years at a 3% annual rate yielding 106.14 million won under semi-annual compounding, creating an effective annual yield of 3.07%.  4. Highlights that compound interest reduces the asset-doubling period compared to simple interest (e.g., 24 years instead of 33 years at a 3% rate).
dict_content: Compound interest is a method of calculating interest on the sum of the principal and the interest earned over a certain period. For example, if you deposit 100 million won in a fixed-term deposit for 2 years at an annual interest rate of 3% with semi-annual compounding (interest is added to the principal every 6 months), the principal and interest after 2 years will be 106.14 million won [100 million won (1 + 3%/2)^4]. In this case, the effective annual yield is 3.07% (6.14%/2). In the above example, you earn 140,000 won more in interest by compounding than with simple interest. The effect of compounding, simply put, is based on the principle that interest earns interest, so as time passes, the additional interest portion increases, and the total principal and interest grow exponentially. Therefore, if the savings period is short, the effect of compounding is not significant, while the longer the savings period, even a small difference in interest rates (since compound interest is higher than simple interest) results in a significantly larger amount of interest. In compounding, there is the Rule of 72. When interest is compounded, since the principal and interest grow, the product of the savings period and the interest rate required to double the principal and interest does not need to be 100%, but only 72%. In the above example, the period required to double 100 million won is about 33 years in the case of simple interest (100 million won / 3 million won), whereas in the case of compound interest, it takes 24 years (72% / 3%), so the period to double 100 million won is 9 years shorter with compound interest than with simple interest. The reason we emphasize consistent saving is because the economic outcome of savings is driven by the hidden effect of compounding.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines compound interest simply as "earning more interest over time," failing to explain the structural mechanism of interest being added back into the principal. 2. The student assumes that the compound interest effect is equally powerful across all investment horizons, ignoring the role of the time variable.

name: exchange rate
definition: The exchange rate is the price or ratio at which one country's domestic currency can be converted or exchanged into the currency of another country. It serves as the fundamental mechanism that enables international trade, finance, and cross-border transactions by standardizing the relative value between different national currencies.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Determines specific conversion ratios between major currency pairs, such as the amount of Korean Won exchanged per US Dollar, or Japanese Yen per Euro.  2. Functions as a prerequisite step that must occur before physical or financial transactions between different nations can take place.
dict_content: To conduct transactions with foreign countries, it is necessary to first convert the domestic currency into the currency of the other country. In this way, in transactions between countries, currency exchange must occur first for the transaction to take place, and the rate at which domestic currency is exchanged for foreign currency is called the exchange rate. How much won will be exchanged for dollars, or how much Japanese yen will be exchanged for euros, is all determined according to the exchange rate.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines the exchange rate as simply "the value of money," omitting the core relational aspect of comparing two distinct national currencies. 2. The student assumes that exchange rates only apply to domestic-to-foreign currency pairs, failing to recognize that exchange rates also govern transactions between two entirely foreign entities.

name: consumer price index
definition: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a macroeconomic indicator designed to comprehensively track and measure changes in the price level of a representative basket of goods and services purchased by typical households. It is normalized against a designated base year set at 100 and serves as a fundamental benchmark for evaluating consumer purchasing power, assessing shifts in the cost of living, and calculating adjustments to real wages over time.
acceptable_extensions: 1. In South Korea, it is officially compiled and published by Statistics Korea.  2. The precise item composition and relative weights within the survey basket are adjusted periodically to reflect evolving economic conditions.  3. The index calculations are based on consumer purchase prices collected for approximately 500 specific goods and services that represent a significant share of expenditure across a broad sample of about 40 households.  4. Commonly utilized as an objective, empirical baseline during labor negotiations to determine appropriate wage increases that offset declines in real wages caused by inflation.
dict_content: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a price index compiled to comprehensively track price fluctuations of various goods and services purchased by general households to maintain their consumption lifestyles. Korea's CPI is compiled by Statistics Korea and is based on a base year set to 100. The composition and weighting of the goods and services surveyed are also periodically adjusted to suit economic conditions. Currently, it is based on consumer purchase prices surveyed for approximately 500 items of goods and services that account for a significant portion of the total consumption expenditure of about 40 households. Because the CPI reflects changes in the income or consumption amount necessary for consumers to maintain a certain standard of living, it is used to measure consumer purchasing power and the cost of living. Furthermore, since a rise in the CPI implies a decline in real wages, it is widely used as a basis for wage increases aimed at compensating for this decline.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines CPI broadly as tracking "all prices in the economy," omitting the restriction that it strictly measures items purchased by end consumers or general households. 2. The student treats the CPI basket and item weights as permanent or static constants, failing to realize that consumer lifestyles and purchasing patterns adapt over time.

name: producer price index
definition: The Producer Price Index (PPI) is a macroeconomic indicator that measures the average price fluctuations of goods and services traded between firms at the initial transaction stage within the domestic market. It tracks the base prices actually received by domestic producers and functions as a general-purpose index that reflects the broader supply and demand trends influencing the general price level before goods reach final consumers.
acceptable_extensions: 1. The scope of subject items is exceptionally broad, which allows the index to capture wholesale supply and demand pressures comprehensively.  2. Evaluates the actual revenue received per unit of product by producers, excluding downstream retail markups and transportation margins added later in the distribution chain.  3. In South Korea, this specific economic indicator has been historically compiled and maintained by the Bank of Korea since its inception in 1910.
dict_content: As a price index compiled to measure average price fluctuations of goods and services traded between firms at the first transaction stage of the domestic market, it possesses the character of a general-purpose index because its broad scope of subject items allows it to measure changes in general price levels that reflect overall supply and demand trends of goods and services. The prices used to compile the index are prices at the first transaction stage, that is, the base price actually received by producers per unit of product. The Producer Price Index has been compiled by the Bank of Korea since 1910.
key_terms: {"first transaction stage", "general-purpose index", "supply and demand trends", "bank of korea"}
defense_prompt: 1. The student fails to specify that the PPI captures prices at the first transaction stage, confusing it with prices paid by consumers or mid-tier distributors. 2. The student interprets the PPI narrowly as just an internal tracking tool for factory owners, rather than a leading general-purpose indicator for the whole economy.

name: monetary policy
definition: Monetary policy refers to the strategic macroeconomic policy designed and implemented by a central bank using its exclusive authority to control the money supply or adjust policy interest rates. Its foundational objectives are to maintain price stability and safeguard financial stability, thereby fostering conditions conducive to sustainable economic growth.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Developed historically as an active macroeconomic tool after nations abandoned the gold standard following the Great Depression of the 1930s, allowing currency issuance to be decoupled from physical gold reserves.  2. Originally, central banks focused on narrower administrative tasks such as managing government funds and protecting the banking system rather than steering the macroeconomy.  3. The institutional emphasis on price stability as the primary goal of monetary policy became firmly solidified globally following the severe stagflation and inflation caused by the two oil shocks of the 1970s.
dict_content: Monetary policy refers to the policy implemented by a central bank, which possesses the exclusive power to issue currency, to influence the money supply or interest rates in order to achieve price stability and financial stability, thereby enabling the economy to achieve sustainable growth. Central banks did not implement such monetary policies from the very beginning. It can be said that it was only after many countries abandoned the gold standard in the wake of the Great Depression of the 1930s that central banks, which initially played a primary role in managing government funds and protecting the banking system, began to seek macroeconomic stability through an appropriate level of money supply in response to changing economic conditions. From that point on, central banks were able to issue currency decoupled from gold and supply money at their discretion. Amidst this, as it became known that the money supply and prices are closely related, stabilizing prices by curbing the reckless supply of money became the generalized and universally accepted primary objective of monetary policy. In particular, as the world economy experienced the harmful effects of severe inflation due to two oil crises in the 1970s, the importance of price stability as a goal of monetary policy became more firmly established, and monetary policy became established as one of macroeconomic policies.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines monetary policy solely as a tool to maximize economic growth, omitting the explicit mandates of maintaining price and financial stability. 2. The student assumes that a central bank can freely implement modern discretionary monetary policy even under a strict commodity-backed monetary regime like the gold standard.

name: central bank
definition: A central bank is a unique monetary authority possessing the exclusive power to issue national currency and manage the aggregate money supply, interest rates, and exchange rates. It serves dual operational roles as the "bank of banks" (providing liquidity to financial institutions) and the "bank of the government" (managing state revenues and expenditures), while actively implementing monetary policies and macroprudential measures to achieve the overarching goals of price stability and financial system stability.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Actively serves as the lender of last resort to prevent systemic collapse during severe financial liquidity crises.  2. Historically evolved from institutions like the Bank of England (established in 1694), which transitioned from a monopoly commercial bank into the progenitor of modern central banking architectures.  3. Shifted its primary mandate in the 20th century from gold-backed currency administration to discretionary macroeconomic stabilization following the abolition of the gold standard.  4. Institutionalized policy neutrality during the 1970s and 1980s to combat stagflation, oil shocks, and foreign debt crises.  5. Transitioned away from rigid money supply targeting in the 1990s due to financial liberalization, adopting explicit price stability targeting frameworks instead.  6. Strengthened its macroprudential oversight functions globally following structural vulnerabilities exposed by the 2008 global financial crisis.
dict_content: Generally, based on its exclusive power to issue currency, a central bank performs the banking function of a bank by lending funds to financial institutions to cover shortages, as well as the banking function of the government by managing government revenue and expenditure and lending funds when necessary. Furthermore, it promotes macroeconomic stability, including price stability, by controlling the money supply and interest rates, while also contributing to financial stability through its role as the lender of last resort and macroprudential policies. Central banks did not perform all these functions from the beginning; various functions were added as they evolved alongside economic development. The Bank of England, established in 1694, can be cited as the progenitor of the central bank. At the time, the Bank of England was a commercial bank, but it was granted a monopoly on currency issuance while performing the role of a government bank, and gradually expanded its banking functions to take on its modern form. Since the 20th century, with the abolition of the gold standard and the increasing importance of proper currency management, monetary and credit policy—aimed at promoting macroeconomic stability, including price stability, through the management of the money supply, interest rates, and exchange rates—has become the core function of the central bank. During the 1970s and 1980s, efforts to stabilize the macroeconomic environment were intensified in response to price instability and economic recession caused by the oil crisis and foreign debt crisis; in this process, institutional improvements were made to enhance the neutrality of monetary and credit policy. Since the 1990s, as money supply management showed limitations due to factors such as financial liberalization and the emergence of new financial products, many central banks, including the Bank of Korea, introduced price stability targeting systems. Meanwhile, as the importance of macroprudential policy grew following the 2008 global financial crisis, institutional reforms were implemented by central banks in various countries, including the United States, to strengthen their financial stability functions.
key_terms: {"lender of last resort", "monetary and credit policy", "price stability targeting", "macroprudential policy"}
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines a central bank purely by its standard commercial operations—like lending money and managing deposits—omitting its unique sovereign powers and macroeconomic mandates. 2. The student views the central bank's policy frameworks as static, failing to understand why tools shifted from direct money supply control to explicit inflation targeting or macroprudential policy.

name: foreign exchange reserves
definition: Official Reserve Assets refer to highly liquid, convertible, and marketable external financial assets held directly by a nation's central bank or government. These assets are maintained to adjust balance of payments imbalances, intervene in foreign exchange markets to stabilize the domestic currency, preserve national creditworthiness, and empower the monetary authority to act as a lender of last resort during external credit crises.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Composed primarily of highly secure, high-capacity assets such as foreign currency deposits, foreign government bonds, and foreign securities.  2. Functions as an emergency liquidity buffer to stabilize the domestic acceptance market when a country faces credit rating downgrades or international borrowing constraints.  3. Generates investment profits for the central bank through foreign currency asset management.  4. Creates potential domestic fiscal burdens, specifically concerning the interest payments required on monetary stabilization bonds issued to absorb excess domestic liquidity resulting from reserve accumulation.  5. Serves as the foundational baseline for structural debates regarding the optimal size of a nation's foreign exchange reserves.
dict_content: Official Reserve Assets include convertible, manageable, or marketable external payment reserves held by the central bank or government to offset balance of payments imbalances or to stabilize trading markets. These reserve assets are reserve assets of a nature similar to those required for emergency reporting; since they can be used as a resource to stabilize the acceptance market in the event of foreign credit ratings, they serve as a resource that enables the central bank, etc., to act as a lender of last resort in credit crisis situations where borrowing by financial institutions is required. The fact that assets such as foreign currency deposits, government bonds, and securities deposits are excluded from relational reserves for this purpose implies that they possess high capacity. While domestic reserves act as a safety net during economic crises and help maintain national creditworthiness, the central bank benefits from the profits generated for foreign currency asset investors, but concerns also arise regarding interest payments on monetary stabilization bonds. Consequently, a discussion regarding the size of the reserve assets has begun.
key_terms: {"balance of payments", "lender of last resort", "monetary stabilization bonds", "national creditworthiness"}

The student defines official reserve assets simply as "any foreign money owned by a country," missing the critical criteria of high liquidity, marketability, and direct control by the central bank or government. 2.The student assumes that accumulating an infinite amount of official reserve assets is always entirely beneficial for an economy, overlooking the sterilization costs involved.

name: gross domestic product
definition: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total market value of all final goods and services or gross value added produced by all economic agents within a country's geographic territory over a specific period. It acts as the primary measure of domestic production, capturing economic output regardless of the nationality of the producers, and is calculated as Nominal GDP (at current prices) to gauge economic scale or Real GDP (at constant base-year prices) to analyze actual economic growth and business cycles.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Production activities encompass all participating economic agents, explicitly including households, private firms, and the government sector.  2. Includes all economic income generated by and paid to non-residents (foreign nationals) who are residing and operating within the nation's territorial borders.  3. Nominal GDP utilizes current market prices, making it ideal for mapping the contemporary structure and nominal scale of the national economy.  4. Real GDP eliminates the distorting effects of inflation by utilizing fixed base-year prices, rendering it the standard metric for tracking structural economic growth rates.
dict_content: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the sum of value added or final products created by all economic agents(including households, firms, and the government) participating in production activities within a country's territory over a specific period, evaluated at market prices; this includes income paid to non-residents (foreigners) residing within the country. Meanwhile, depending on the pricing method applied, it is classified into Nominal GDP and Real GDP. Nominal GDP is used to understand the scale and structure of the national economy, while Real GDP is used to analyze the flow of overall economic activity, such as economic growth and business cycles.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines GDP simply as "the total income earned by a country's citizens," failing to distinguish between the territorial boundaries of GDP and the nationality boundaries of Gross National Income. 2. The student fails to realize the difference between nominal and real values, assuming that a higher Nominal GDP automatically means a nation produced more physical goods and services.

name: unemployment rate
definition: The economically active population (or labor force) represents the segment of the working-age population that is both able and willing to provide labor for the production of goods and services during a specific reference period. It serves as the primary baseline for evaluating nationwide employment conditions and is structurally categorized into two mutually exclusive groups: employed persons and unemployed persons.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Differentiated strictly from the non-economically active population, who are classified as individuals unwilling or unable to engage in economic activities at the time of the survey.  2. Evaluated through the labor force participation rate, which calculates the percentage of the working-age population that constitutes the economically active population.  3. Survey frameworks analyze demographic variables, such as age and residential structures, to determine the underlying population capable of creating and entering the active labor force.  4. Inclusion in statistics depends on the population being clearly present and possessing the immediate physical or mental capability to provide labor during the specific survey window.
dict_content: When assessing employment conditions, the population engaged in economically productive activities holds greater significance than the total population. Employment statistics, which are compiled continuously, are based on the population available over a specific period; this population is further divided into the economically active population, who are willing to participate in existing economic activities, and the non-economically active population, who are unwilling to engage in economic activities. The reason the economically active population is included—whether for the purpose of utilizing manpower or for the purpose of the survey—is that they are clearly present at the time of the survey and are capable of engaging in economic activities to provide the ability to do so. The activity participation rate, which measures the existence of the population passing through the employment status survey, the economically active population, and the types of available labor force such as employed and unemployed persons, and enables the residential structure based on factors such as age, is considered as the population capable of creating the economically active population, and the participation rate is treated as the economically active population.
key_terms: {"economically active population", "non-economically active population", "employed persons", "unemployed persons", "labor force participation rate"}
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines the economically active population simply as "everyone who has a job in a country," completely omitting individuals who are actively looking for work. 2. The student fails to establish the boundary of 'willingness and capability,' leading to a misclassification of the non-economically active population.

name: stagflation
definition: Stagflation is a macroeconomic anomaly characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of economic stagnation (recession or a declining growth rate of national income) and high inflation (persistently rising general price levels). It defies traditional business cycle models by combining a contracting economy with increasing costs, resulting in severe economic hardship for individuals and businesses alike.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Historically manifested prominently during the 1970s, triggered globally by major supply-side disruptions such as the second oil crisis.  2. Breaks the historical pre-World War II economic pattern where prices typically fell during recessions and rose exclusively during economic booms.  3. Often aggravated by supply-side shocks—such as sudden surges in production costs (e.g., energy, raw materials, or institutional fees)—which run counter to declining aggregate demand.
dict_content: Prior to World War II, it was generally the case that water gradually decreased during economic recessions and prices rose during economic booms. However, after World War II, the country experienced a second oil crisis in the 1970s, and it began with the realization that influencers exist even during the backup period. A situation where inflation increases simultaneously due to these factors is called stagflation. Stagflation is a condition characterized by the persistence of stagnation (economic recession) and inflation (rising prices). In other words, it is a phenomenon where inflation—driven by tuition fees that run counter to an economy where the growth rate of national income is declining—occurs simultaneously. Due to both the mistakes that lead to stagflation and the inflation rate, people's economic hardship will be significant.
defense_prompt: 1. The student explains stagflation using traditional demand-pull framework assumptions, where rising prices must imply a overheating, booming economy. 2. The student focuses exclusively on monetary expansion as the cause, ignoring the critical role of negative supply shocks or structural cost increases.

name: bank run
definition: A bank run is a sudden financial crisis where a large number of anxious depositors simultaneously withdraw their funds from a financial institution due to fears regarding its management, solvency, or overall systemic stability. Because banks operate on a fractional reserve system and lack the immediate cash reserves to pay out all deposits at once, this panic can trigger severe liquidity shortages and drive an otherwise solvent bank into actual insolvency.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Actively mitigated by state-backed deposit insurance companies designed to restore consumer confidence and neutralize systemic panic.  2. In South Korea, deposits are legally protected up to a statutory limit of 50 million won per depositor per financial institution under the Depositor Protection Act.  3. Frequently acts as a primary leading indicator or catalyst for broader economic contractions and banking panics during periods of severe financial instability.
dict_content: It displays the deposit withdrawal indicator during the expansion period. If financial conditions are unstable or problems arise with a bank's management and soundness, the bank may be in a state of panic as it does not have funds available to pay out, as depositors may be unable to receive their money. This is called a bank run, and deposit insurance companies have protected deposits of up to 50 million won under the Depositor Protection Act to prevent certain instability and respond to bank runs.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines a bank run as a situation occurring only when a bank has already lost all its assets through bad investments, ignoring the psychological and self-fulfilling nature of the panic. 2. The student assumes that deposit insurance completely eliminates all risks for financial institutions, failing to see the moral hazard or systemic limitations of a safety net.

name: liquidity
definition: Liquidity is an economic metric representing the ease and speed with which an asset can be converted into cash without experiencing a significant loss in value. It spans asset liquidity (the exchangeability of non-monetary assets into money and subsequently into goods) and economic agent liquidity (an entity's capacity to settle its financial obligations), and often functions as a synonym for money itself or as the foundational criteria used to classify different monetary aggregates based on their closeness to cash.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Asset liquidity is structurally influenced by market formation, transaction mechanisms, asset quality/quantity, and refinancing avenues.  2. In South Korea, monetary and liquidity indicators are officially structured in descending order of liquidity into Cash, M1 (Narrow Money), M2 (Broad Money), Lf (Liquidity of Financial Institutions), and L (Liquidity Aggregates).  3. The term is colloquially used interchangeably with currency itself in macroeconomic phrases like "abundant market liquidity" or "liquidity supply policies by the Bank of Korea."
dict_content: Liquidity is a term indicating the degree to which assets can be converted into cash, representing the extent to which a company's assets can be exchanged for money without loss when needed. Liquidity is divided into asset liquidity and economic agent liquidity; asset liquidity is further divided into monetary liquidity and liquidity of non-monetary assets. Monetary liquidity refers to the extent to which money can be converted into other goods or services. Asset liquidity refers to the extent to which non-monetary assets can be converted into other goods or services after being converted into money. The degree of asset liquidity varies depending on the quantity and quality of the assets subject to conversion, market formation, transaction methods, and the possibility of refinancing. Meanwhile, economic agent liquidity refers to the ability of each economic agent to cover its debts. Derived from the original meaning described above, this concept of liquidity is also used in the following two forms. First, liquidity is used as a criterion to distinguish where to draw the line between cash in circulation and various financial instruments as currency. In Korea, monetary and liquidity indicators are classified into cash currency, M1, M2, Lf, and L based on the level of liquidity. Secondly, liquidity is sometimes used interchangeably with highly liquid currency itself, including cash. In examples such as “abundant liquidity in the market” or “liquidity supply policies implemented by the Bank of Korea,” liquidity refers to currency itself.
defense_prompt: 1. The student defines liquidity solely as the speed of converting an asset to cash, neglecting the condition that the conversion must occur without significant loss of value. 2. The student confuses monetary aggregates, assuming that broader financial instruments like M2 or Lf have higher liquidity than narrow cash reserves due to their massive scale.

name: open market operations
definition: Open market operations (OMO) are a flexible monetary policy tool used by a central bank to manage market liquidity and steer short-term interest rates toward its official base rate target. This is achieved by systematically buying or selling financial securities, such as government bonds or repurchase agreements (RPs), directly with commercial financial institutions within the open market, thereby altering the volume of reserves available in the banking system.
acceptable_extensions: 1. Highly favored by developed central banks due to its market-friendly nature, operating through existing price mechanisms, and allowing for immediate, flexible adjustments to timing and scale.  2. Contrasted structurally with more rigid, administrative policy alternatives like shifting statutory reserve requirements or modifying direct lending/deposit window facilities.  3. In South Korea, the Bank of Korea utilizes OMO to tightly bind the interbank call rate to the base rate by managing surplus or deficit reserve positions.  4. Compared to other monetary policy tools (such as reserve requirements and lending/deposit systems), open market operations allow for flexible determination of timing and scale. Furthermore, because they are market-friendly as they operate according to the price mechanisms of the financial market and enable rapid policy implementation through immediate trading transactions, most central banks in developed countries use open market operations as their primary monetary policy tool.
